cards.note: Bicycle signs in Czechia are yellow.
Czech sign posts typically have thick, black caps.

Czechia uses arrow-shaped directional signs with a filled in tip. Due to the shape, they are recognizable from behind.

NOTE: Slovakia has small white arrows instead.

While rare, it is possible to find Generation 2 in Czechia.

NOTE: Slovakia does not have any Generation 2.

Much of Czech Generation 3 coverage was taken during winter, resulting in very grey, and occasionally snowy, coverage.

NOTE: This is not common in Slovakia.

Czech highway signs can be either blue or green, and have a thin white border, which is separated from the edge by a second coloured border.

NOTE: Slovak highway signs have a white border right on the edge.
House numbers in Czechia are generally written on blue or red signs with thin white borders.
Czech kilometre markers have a yellow outline outside the black frame and do not have a black horizontal middle line.
Czech distinctly uses the letters Ř, Ě and Ů. NOTE: Acute accents on vowels are not found in South Slavic languages.
Czech railway crossing signs do not have a background.

The borders of Czech road signs are almost always separated from the edge by a strip in the same colour as the sign background.

NOTE: In Slovakia, it is more common for signs to have the border on the edge of the sign.

Czechia often has solid outer roadlines, with no centre line.

NOTE: While these roadlines can be found in all neighbouring countries, it is notably also common in Germany.
The Czech landscape is fairly rolling, with a lot of hills and altitude changes, but not a lot of tall mountains. Generally speaking, Slovakia has more mountains, but also more completely flat areas.

Suburban houses in Czechia are commonly connected in pairs.

NOTE: This is less common in most neighbouring countries, including Slovakia.

In Czechia, street signs are typically bright red —either wide and wall-mounted or thin and on posts. Blue variants are also common. The Czech word for street is “ulice” (not “ulica”), though it's often omitted. In contrast, Slovakia uses white signs with red borders and blue text.
Slovak road signs normally feature a very bold font.
Wooden poles and white concrete supports are more common in Slovakia than in Czechia. However, due to variability, this detail is preferably used for tough 50/50 decisions.
Slovakia uses blue directional signs, with small white arrows.

It is fairly common to see small signs with double sign posts in Slovakia.

NOTE: While large signs may have double sign posts, small signs rarely do in Czechia.

Grey metal roofs are very common, particularly in the eastern parts of Slovakia.

NOTE: Apart from the most mountainous areas, it is far less common in Czechia.
Slovak highway signs can be either blue or green, and have a white border right at the edge of the sign.
House numbers in Slovakia are typically written on white signs with a thin red or black border.
Slovak kilometre markers typically have two sections divided with a black horizontal line. The top section contains the road number.

cards.a: Slovakia - Ľ, Ô, Ä, Ŕ and Ĺ
cards.note: Slovakia distinctly uses the letters Ľ, Ô, Ä, Ŕ and Ĺ.
Slovakia recently adopted a new bollard design similar to Hungary’s: a wedge-shaped European style with a red front reflector. Currently, it's still rarely seen.
The Slovak railway crossing sign has a white rectangular background.
Slovak road signs commonly have the painted sign border right at the edge of the sign.
The top of Slovak sign posts are typically either open, have a grey metal cap or a thin black cap.
White street signs with blue text and a thin red border are by far the most common in Slovakia.
The Slovak landscape varies between very mountainous and completely flat. Generally speaking, Czechia is hillier, but less mountainous.
